subject: history
title: Rivers, cities, and the first states
objective: Connect settlement, surplus, specialized work, records, and authority while separating evidence from inference.

lesson.opening: Early cities grew through connected changes rather than one automatic chain. Environmental conditions shaped choices, while institutions and people organized work in different ways.

sections.heading: Start with the setting
sections.body: Rivers could support farming and transport, but they also brought floods, drought, and disputes over water. A historical explanation should name the environmental feature before claiming what it caused.

sections.heading: Trace a possible sequence
sections.body: A surplus of food could support coordinated labor and specialized work. Record keeping might then help institutions track goods and obligations. This is a model to test, not a universal rule.

sections.heading: Separate evidence from inference
sections.body: A storehouse, tablet, or settlement layer is evidence. The claim that it proves a particular political arrangement is an inference. Good history marks that boundary and asks what other evidence would support it.

sections.heading: Compare sources carefully
sections.body: A building record and a later narrative may describe the same society for different purposes. Compare what each source preserves, what it leaves out, and who had reason to create it.

activities.prompt: Which statement names the environmental setting before claiming what it caused?
choices: The Nile flooded predictably, which could support farming.
Egypt was the first true civilization.
Kings caused all early cities to grow.
activities.hint: A good explanation names the condition, then the consequence.

activities.prompt: Arrange this account from material condition to political consequence.
activities.instructions: Treat this as a reasoned model, not a claim that every city followed one automatic path.

activities.prompt: Which of these is evidence rather than an inference?
choices: A storehouse floor and sealed accounting tablets
The ruler owned all the land
Trade was the city's main goal
activities.hint: Evidence can be observed in the remains; an inference interprets them.

activities.prompt: When comparing two sources about the same society, what should you examine first?
choices: What each source preserves and leaves out
Which account agrees with your view
activities.hint: Ask who created each source and for what purpose.

activities.prompt: Which statement treats the sequence of change as a testable model rather than a universal rule?
choices: Surplus may have supported specialized work in some cities.
Record keeping caused every early state.
activities.hint: A model can be supported or challenged by further evidence.

activities.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between evidence and inference, using one example from this lesson.
activities.instructions: Name the evidence, then state the inference it might support and what could test it.
activities.context: A storehouse floor, a tablet, or a settlement layer is evidence you can observe. The claim that it proves a particular political arrangement is an inference. Ask what other surviving evidence would support or challenge that inference.
